Michmash, about 7 miles (11 km) north of Jerusalem (1 Samuel 13–14).

verses.text: In the year 160 (152 BC){a} Alexander Epiphanes, son of Antiochus,{b} came up and took Ptolemais. The people welcomed him, and he began to reign there.
Hearing of it, King Demetrius mustered a very large army and marched out to give him battle.
Demetrius also sent Jonathan a letter couched in peaceable terms, meant to raise him in honor.
"Let us move first," he reasoned, "and make peace with them before Jonathan makes peace with Alexander against us.
For he will remember every wrong we did to him, to his brothers, and to his nation."
So he gave Jonathan authority to raise troops and to equip them with arms as his ally, and he gave word that the hostages held in the citadel were to be released into his hands.
Jonathan came to Jerusalem and read the letter aloud in the hearing of all the people and of the men in the citadel.
These were struck with great fear when they heard that the king had given him authority to raise troops.
The men of the citadel surrendered the hostages to Jonathan, and he gave them back to their parents.
Jonathan took up residence in Jerusalem and set about building and restoring the city.
He told those doing the work to rebuild the walls and to ring Mount Zion with squared stones for defense, and so they did.
Then the foreigners in the strongholds Bacchides had built took flight;
each of them abandoned his post and went back to his own country.
Only in Beth-zur did some remain of those who had forsaken the law and the commandments, for it served them as a refuge.

King Alexander heard of all the promises Demetrius had sent to Jonathan, and he was told of the battles and brave deeds that Jonathan and his brothers had performed and the hardships they had endured.
"Shall we ever find another man like this?" he said. "Let us make him our friend and ally at once."
So he wrote a letter and sent it to him in these words:
"King Alexander to his brother Jonathan, greetings.
Word has reached us about you, that you are a man of might and valor, well fitted to be our friend.

So we appoint you this day high priest of your nation; you are to bear the title Friend of the King, to take our side, and to keep friendship with us." He also sent him a purple robe and a golden crown.
So Jonathan put on the sacred vestments in the seventh month (in September–October) of the year 160 (152 BC),{c} at the Festival of Booths,{d} and he raised troops and laid in a great supply of arms.
When Demetrius heard of these things, he was vexed and said,
"What have we done, that Alexander has outrun us in winning the friendship of the Jews to strengthen himself?
I too will write them words of encouragement, with offers of honors and gifts, so that they may stand by me as helpers."

So he sent them this message:
"King Demetrius to the nation of the Jews, greetings.
You have kept your covenant with us and remained in our friendship, and have not gone over to our enemies. We have heard of this and are glad.
Now go on keeping faith with us, and we will repay you with good things for what you do for us.
Many exemptions will we grant you, and gifts besides.
"I now release you and free all the Jews from tribute, from the salt tax, and from the crown levies.{e}

Instead of a third of the grain and half the fruit of the trees that is due to me, I release them from this day on, so that they will no longer be collected from Judah's land, nor from the three districts joined to it out of Samaria and Galilee,{f} from now until the end of time.
Let Jerusalem and her territory be holy and free from tax, both tithes and tolls.
I give up also my authority over the citadel in Jerusalem, and I grant it to the high priest, to post there whatever men he himself may choose as its guard.
Every Jew carried captive out of Judah's land into any region of my realm I release as free, without ransom; and let all officials cancel the taxes on their livestock as well.
All festivals, sabbaths, new moons, and appointed days, and the three days before a festival and the three days after it, shall be days of immunity and release for all the Jews in my kingdom.
No one shall have authority to exact payment from any of them or to trouble them in any matter.
"Let Jews be enrolled in the king's forces, to the number of thirty thousand men, and let them receive pay as is due to all the king's forces.

Some of them shall be stationed in the king's great strongholds, and some appointed to positions of trust in the kingdom. Their officers and leaders shall be of their own number, and they shall live by their own laws, as the king has commanded in the land of Judah.
The three districts added to Judea from the region of Samaria are to be annexed to Judea and reckoned under one ruler, obeying no other authority than the high priest.
Ptolemais and the land belonging to it I give as a gift to the holy place in Jerusalem, to defray what the sanctuary must spend.
I also grant each year about 375 pounds of silver{g} from the royal revenues out of the places that belong to me.
And all the surplus that the officials did not pay over as in former years they shall from now on give for the work on the temple.
Moreover, the 125 pounds of silver{h} that they used to take each year from the sanctuary's income are also released, because they belong to the priests who minister there.

Whoever takes refuge at the temple in Jerusalem or anywhere within its precincts, because he owes money to the king or for any other debt, shall be released, together with all his property in my kingdom.
For the rebuilding and restoring of the structures of the sanctuary, the cost shall be paid from the king's revenues.
And for rebuilding the walls of Jerusalem and fortifying it all around, the cost shall be paid from the king's revenues, as also for rebuilding the walls in Judea."

When Jonathan and the people heard these words, they put no faith in them and would not accept them, for they remembered the great evil Demetrius had done in Israel and how sorely he had oppressed them.
Alexander had their goodwill, for he was the one who had first opened talk of peace with them, and they remained his allies all his days.
King Alexander gathered large forces and encamped opposite Demetrius.
The two kings joined battle, and Demetrius's army fled. Alexander pursued him and overpowered them.{i}
He pressed the battle hard until the sun went down, and Demetrius fell that day.
Then Alexander sent envoys to Ptolemy king of Egypt{j} with this message:
"I have returned to my kingdom and taken my seat on the throne of my ancestors. I have established my rule; I have crushed Demetrius and taken possession of our country.
I met him in battle; he was beaten by us, he and his host, and the throne of his realm is now ours.
Now let us establish friendship with each other. Give me your daughter in marriage; I will be joined to you by marriage and give you and her gifts worthy of you."
King Ptolemy replied, "Happy the day you returned to the land of your ancestors and took your seat on the throne of their kingdom!
What you have written I will now do. Come to Ptolemais, though, where we can meet face to face, and there I will give you my daughter, just as you ask."
So Ptolemy set out from Egypt with his daughter Cleopatra{k} and came to Ptolemais in the year 162 (150 BC).{l}
King Alexander met him there; Ptolemy gave him his daughter Cleopatra, and celebrated her wedding at Ptolemais with great pomp, as kings do.
Then a letter came from King Alexander inviting Jonathan to a meeting.
Jonathan went in splendor to Ptolemais and met the two kings. He gave them and their Friends silver and gold and many gifts, and he won their favor.
A band of scoundrels from Israel, lawless men, gathered against him to bring charges against him, but the king paid them no heed.
Instead the king gave orders that Jonathan be stripped of his garments and clothed in purple, and so it was done.
The king seated him at his side and said to his officers, "Go with him into the heart of the city and make it known that none may accuse him about anything or harass him for any reason."
When his accusers saw the honor paid him, as was proclaimed, and saw him clothed in purple, they all fled.
So the king honored him: he entered his name among the First Friends and appointed him general and governor of a province.{m}
And Jonathan went home to Jerusalem in peace and with joy.
In the year 165 (147 BC){n} Demetrius son of Demetrius{o} came from Crete to the land of his ancestors.
When King Alexander heard of it, he was greatly troubled and went back to Antioch.
Demetrius appointed Apollonius, governor of Coelesyria,{p} who gathered a large force and camped at Jamnia. He sent this message to Jonathan the high priest:
"You alone are standing up against us, and I have become a laughingstock and a reproach because of you. Why do you lord it over us in the hills?
If you trust in your forces, come down to us in the plain, and let us test each other there, for I have with me the strength of the cities.
Inquire and find out who I am, and who else stands with us. They will tell you that you cannot stand your ground before us, for your ancestors were twice put to flight in their own land.{q}
And now you will not be able to withstand cavalry and such a force as this in the plain, where there is no stone or pebble and no place to flee."
When Jonathan heard Apollonius's words, he was stirred to anger. He chose out ten thousand men and marched from Jerusalem, and Simon his brother came to join him with help.
He camped before Joppa, but its people shut him out, because Apollonius had a garrison in Joppa. So they attacked it,
and the people of the city, afraid, opened the gates, and Jonathan took possession of Joppa.

Hearing this, Apollonius set in array three thousand horsemen and a great army and marched toward Azotus as though passing through, while at the same time he advanced into the plain, because he had a large force of cavalry and relied on it.
Jonathan pursued him to Azotus, and the armies joined battle.
Now Apollonius had left a thousand cavalry hidden behind them.
Jonathan learned that there was an ambush behind him. The enemy encircled his army and from dawn till late in the day rained arrows on his men.
But his men stood firm, as Jonathan had ordered, and the enemy's horses grew tired.
Then Simon brought up his force and engaged the phalanx, for the cavalry was exhausted. The enemy were crushed by him and fled.
The cavalry scattered over the plain; they fled to Azotus and went into Beth-dagon, the temple of their idol,{r} to save themselves.
But Jonathan burned Azotus and the towns around it and plundered them. The temple of Dagon he burned with fire, and its sacred precinct too.{s}
Those who fell by the sword, together with those burned, numbered about eight thousand men.
From there Jonathan set out and camped against Askalon, and its people came out to meet him with great honor.
Then Jonathan returned to Jerusalem with his men, laden with much spoil.
These reports moved King Alexander to heap further honors on Jonathan.
He sent him a golden buckle, such as is customarily given to the King's Kinsmen,{t} and he gave him Ekron and all its territory as his possession.

notes.text: Greek: in the 160th year (Seleucid era; see note on 1:10).
Alexander Balas, who claimed to be a son of Antiochus IV Epiphanes.
Greek: in the seventh month of the 160th year (Seleucid era; see note on 1:10). The seventh month is Tishri (September–October).
Greek skēnopēgia, "tent-pitching," the Festival of Booths (Tabernacles; Leviticus 23:33–43).
Gifts of gold crowns, originally voluntary, had become a regular tax.
The three districts were Aphairema, Lydda, and Rathamin (11:34). Swete's Greek here has "from Samaria and Galilee"; compare v. 38, which mentions only Samaria.
Greek: fifteen thousand shekels of silver, about 6,000 oz (172 kg); weight standards varied.
Greek: five thousand shekels of silver, about 2,000 oz (57 kg).
Swete's Greek has "Alexander pursued him"; some editors, following the context and Josephus, read that Demetrius pursued Alexander's army. The translation follows Swete.
Ptolemy VI Philometor (reigned 180–145 BC).
Cleopatra Thea, later married in turn to Demetrius II and Antiochus VII.
Greek: in the 162nd year (Seleucid era; see note on 1:10).
Greek meridarchēs, "ruler of a part"; that is, governor of a district.
Greek: in the 165th year (Seleucid era; see note on 1:10).
Demetrius II Nicator, son of Demetrius I.

Coelesyria, "hollow Syria," properly the Beqaa valley, but here used of the whole Seleucid province west of the Euphrates. Swete's Greek reads "Demetrius appointed Apollonius who was over Coelesyria"; some think Apollonius was Alexander's governor who went over to Demetrius.
Perhaps a reference to the defeats of 1 Samuel 4 and 31.
Beth-dagon, "house of Dagon," the Philistine god (1 Samuel 5:1–5).
So Swete's Greek text, literally "and its temple"; some ancient witnesses read "and those who had fled into it."
"Kinsmen" was the highest rank of honor at the Seleucid court.

verses.text: Then the king of Egypt massed forces as countless as the sand along the seashore, along with many ships, and he schemed to seize Alexander's kingdom by trickery and annex it to his own.
He set out for Syria professing peace, and the people of the towns opened their gates and came out to meet him, for King Alexander had commanded them to meet him, since he was his father-in-law.
But whenever Ptolemy entered a town, he left troops behind as a garrison in it.

When he drew near Azotus, they showed him the burned temple of Dagon, Azotus and its suburbs in ruins, the corpses lying about, and the charred remains of those Jonathan had burned in the battle, for they had piled them in heaps along his route.
They told the king what Jonathan had done, hoping to bring blame on him, but the king kept silent.
Jonathan came with ceremony to meet the king at Joppa; they exchanged greetings, and both lodged there that night.
Jonathan went with the king as far as the river called Eleutherus{a} and then returned to Jerusalem.
So King Ptolemy made himself master of the coastal towns as far as Seleucia by the sea,{b} all the while plotting evil against Alexander.
He sent envoys to King Demetrius, saying, "Come, let us make a pact. I will give you my daughter, who is now Alexander's wife, and you shall reign over your father's kingdom.
It grieves me that I ever gave him my daughter, for he has sought my life."
He made these charges against him because he coveted his kingdom.
So he took his daughter away and gave her to Demetrius. He broke with Alexander, and their enmity came into the open.
Then Ptolemy entered Antioch and put on the crown of Asia, so that he wore two crowns on his head, the crown of Egypt and that of Asia.
At that time King Alexander was in Cilicia, because the people of that region were in revolt.
When Alexander heard of these events, he came to make war on him. Ptolemy marched out and met him with a strong force and routed him.
Alexander fled into Arabia to find shelter there, and King Ptolemy was exalted.
Zabdiel the Arab{c} cut off Alexander's head and sent it to Ptolemy.
Yet within three days King Ptolemy himself was dead, and the men he had posted in the strongholds were slain by those who lived there.
So Demetrius became king in the year 167 (145 BC).{d}
At that time Jonathan called together the men of Judea to storm the citadel in Jerusalem, and many engines of siege were set up against it.
But certain lawless men who hated their own nation went to the king and reported that Jonathan was besieging the citadel.
Angered by the news, he broke camp at once and came to Ptolemais. He wrote to Jonathan to lift the siege and to come with all speed to Ptolemais to confer with him.
When Jonathan heard this, he ordered the siege to continue. He chose some of the elders of Israel and some of the priests, and put himself in danger.
With silver and gold, garments, and a wealth of other presents he came before the king at Ptolemais and won his goodwill.
Some lawless men of his nation kept bringing complaints against him,
but the king dealt with him as the kings before him had done and raised him high in the sight of all his Friends.
He confirmed him in the high priesthood and in all the other honors he had held before, and he made him one of his First Friends.
Then Jonathan requested of the king that Judea, together with the three districts and Samaria,{e} be made exempt from tribute, and he promised him about eleven tons of silver.{f}
The king consented and wrote Jonathan a letter about all these matters, as follows:
"King Demetrius to his brother Jonathan and to the nation of the Jews, greetings.
We are sending you also a copy of the letter we wrote about you to Lasthenes, our Kinsman, so that you may know its contents:
'King Demetrius to Lasthenes his father,{g} greetings.
Toward the nation of the Jews, our friends, who keep faith in what they owe us, we are resolved to act generously in return for their goodwill toward us.

We confirm to them the territory of Judea and the three districts of Aphairema, Lydda, and Rathamin;{h} these were added to Judea from Samaria, with all the land belonging to them. To all who sacrifice in Jerusalem this is granted in place of the royal dues the king used to collect from them yearly out of the harvest of the soil and the produce of the orchards.
As for our other revenues from now on, from the tithes and tolls due to us, the salt pans, and the crown levies due to us, all these we remit to them.
None of these grants shall be revoked from now on for all time.
See to it, then, that a copy of these terms is made and given to Jonathan, and set up on the holy mountain in a fitting and conspicuous place.'"

King Demetrius saw that the land was quiet before him and that no one opposed him, so he dismissed all his troops, each to his own home, except the foreign troops he had recruited from the islands of the nations. So all the troops who had served his fathers turned hostile to him.

Now Trypho,{i} who had formerly been one of Alexander's supporters, noticed how the whole army was muttering against Demetrius. He went to Simalkue{j} the Arab, who was bringing up Antiochus, Alexander's young son,
and kept pressing him to hand the boy over, so that he might reign in his father's place. He told him all that Demetrius had done and how his troops hated him, and he stayed there many days.
Meanwhile Jonathan sent to King Demetrius asking him to remove the troops of the citadel from Jerusalem and the troops in the strongholds, for they kept making war on Israel.
Demetrius sent this reply to Jonathan: "These things I will do for you and your people, and more: I will load you and your nation with honor once the moment is right.
So you will act rightly if you send me men to fight at my side, for all my troops have revolted."
So Jonathan sent three thousand stalwart men to him at Antioch. When they came to the king, he was delighted at their arrival.
Then the people of the city massed in the middle of the city, about a hundred twenty thousand of them, intending to kill the king.
The king took refuge in the palace, while the citizens seized the city's streets and began the fight.
So the king called on the Jews for help. They all rallied to him at once, spread out through the city, and that day killed about a hundred thousand in the city.
They set fire to the city, seized much plunder that day, and rescued the king.
When the citizens saw that the Jews had mastered the city as they pleased, they lost heart and cried out to the king with supplication:
"Give us your right hand in peace, and let the Jews cease their war on us and on the city."
They threw down their weapons and made peace. The Jews gained great honor before the king and in the eyes of all in his kingdom, and they returned to Jerusalem with much plunder.
So King Demetrius sat on the throne of his kingdom, and the land was quiet before him.
But he broke every promise he had made. He turned against Jonathan, did not repay the kindnesses Jonathan had shown him, and treated him very harshly.
Some time later Trypho came back, bringing the little boy Antiochus,{k} who took the throne and was crowned.
All the troops whom Demetrius had cast off rallied to him, and they fought against Demetrius, who fled in defeat.
Trypho captured the elephants and took control of Antioch.
Then the young Antiochus wrote to Jonathan: "I confirm you in the high priesthood and set you over the four districts,{l} and you shall be one of the King's Friends."
He sent him gold plate and table service, and gave him leave to drink from golden vessels, to be clothed in purple, and to wear a golden buckle.
His brother Simon he made governor from the Ladder of Tyre{m} to the borders of Egypt.

Then Jonathan set out and traveled through the province Beyond the River and its towns, and the whole Syrian army flocked to him in alliance. At Askalon the townspeople came out and received him with honor.
From there he went to Gaza, but the people of Gaza shut him out. So he besieged it and burned its suburbs and plundered them.

Then the people of Gaza pleaded with Jonathan, and he made peace with them. He took the sons of their rulers as hostages and sent them to Jerusalem. Then he passed through the country as far as Damascus.
News reached Jonathan that the generals of Demetrius were at Kedesh{n} in Galilee with a great force, aiming to oust him from his post.
So he marched against them, but Simon his brother he left behind in the land.
Simon camped against Beth-zur, attacked it for many days, and hemmed it in.
Then they asked him for terms, and he granted them. He expelled them from there, took possession of the town, and set a garrison over it.
Jonathan and his army camped by the waters of Gennesaret,{o} and early in the morning they marched to the plain of Hazor.{p}
There, in the plain, the foreign army came against him. They had hidden men in the hills to fall on him, while their main body came straight at him.
Then the men in ambush rose from their places and joined battle, and all Jonathan's men fled.
Not one of them was left except Mattathias son of Absalom and Judas son of Chalphi, commanders of the army.
Jonathan ripped his garments, threw earth on his head, and prayed.
Then he turned back to battle against the enemy, routed them, and they fled.
Seeing this, the men who had fled from him came back and chased the enemy along with him as far as Kedesh, to the enemy's camp, and there they encamped.
Of the foreigners about three thousand fell that day. Then Jonathan went back to Jerusalem.

notes.text: The Eleutherus (modern Nahr el-Kebir) formed the northern border of Coelesyria.
Seleucia Pieria, the port of Antioch.
Josephus calls him Zabeilos. The Greek Zabdiel means "my gift is God" (Hebrew).
Greek: in the 167th year (Seleucid era; see note on 1:10). Demetrius II became king in 145 BC.
So Swete's Greek text; compare v. 34 and 10:30, 38, where the three districts are themselves taken from Samaria.
Greek: three hundred talents, about 22,500 lb (10,200 kg). Weight standards varied.
"Father" was a court title of honor.
Aphairema (Ephraim, John 11:54), Lydda (Lod, Acts 9:32), and Rathamin (perhaps Ramathaim, 1 Samuel 1:1).
Trypho, "luxury," was the nickname of Diodotus, a general.
So Swete's Greek text; some ancient witnesses read "Imalkue."
Antiochus VI Epiphanes Dionysus, about four years old.
The three districts of v. 34 and perhaps the region around Akrabattene or Perea; uncertain.
The Ladder of Tyre, a headland on the coast north of Ptolemais.
Kedesh in Galilee, northwest of Lake Huleh (Joshua 20:7).
The Sea of Galilee.
Swete's Greek reads "Nasor," probably for Hazor, north of the Sea of Galilee.

verses.text: Seeing that the time was working in his favor, Jonathan chose men and sent them to Rome to confirm and renew the friendship with the Romans.
To the Spartans{a} and to other places too he sent letters to the same effect.
So they journeyed to Rome, entered the Senate chamber, and said, "Jonathan the high priest and the Jewish nation have sent us to renew for them the friendship and alliance as it stood before."
The Romans gave them letters to the authorities in each place, asking them to send the envoys on their way to the land of Judah in peace.
Here is a copy of what Jonathan wrote to the Spartans:
"Jonathan the high priest, the council of elders of the nation, the priests, and all the remaining Jewish people send greetings to the Spartans, their brothers.
Long ago a letter was sent to Onias the high priest from Arius,{b} who was then king among you, stating that you are our brothers, as the attached copy shows.
Onias received the envoy with honor and accepted the letter, in which alliance and friendship were plainly declared.
Now we, though we stand in no need of these, since we take encouragement from the holy books in our hands,
have ventured to send envoys to renew our brotherhood and friendship, lest we grow strangers to you; for many years have passed since your message came to us.

We for our part, at every season and without fail, at our festivals and on the other fitting days, remember you in the sacrifices we offer and in our prayers, as it is right and proper to remember brothers.
And we rejoice in your renown.
But as for us, many troubles and many wars have hemmed us in, and the kings around us have fought against us.
We did not wish to trouble you, nor our other friends and allies, over these wars,
for we have the help that comes from heaven to aid us, and we have been rescued from our enemies, and our enemies have been brought low.
So we have chosen Numenius son of Antiochus and Antipater son of Jason, and have sent them to the Romans to renew our former friendship and alliance with them.
We have instructed them to go to you also, to greet you, and to deliver to you this letter of ours concerning the renewal of our brotherhood.
And now you will do well to send us a reply to this."
This is a copy of the letter that was sent to Onias:
"Arius king of the Spartans to Onias the high priest, greetings.
A writing has come to light about the Spartans and the Jews, showing that the two are brothers, of Abraham's stock.{c}
Now that this is known to us, you will do well to write us of how you fare.
We on our side write to you that your livestock and your property are ours, and ours are yours. We therefore command that our envoys report to you accordingly."
Now Jonathan heard that the commanders of Demetrius had come back with a larger army than before to make war on him.
He marched out from Jerusalem and met them in the region of Hamath,{d} for he gave them no chance to set foot in his own country.
He sent spies into their camp, who came back and reported that the enemy were drawn up to fall upon the Jews by night.
So when the sun had set, Jonathan ordered his men to stay awake and under arms, ready for battle all night long, and he posted sentries around the camp.
When the enemy heard that Jonathan and his men were prepared for battle, they were afraid, their hearts quailed, and they lit fires in their camp.{e}
Jonathan and his men, seeing the fires still alight, knew nothing of it till dawn.
Then Jonathan gave chase, but could not catch them, since they were already across the river Eleutherus.
So Jonathan turned aside against the Arabs called Zabadeans,{f} struck them down, and took their spoil.
Then he broke camp, came to Damascus, and marched through all that region.
Simon too set out and marched as far as Askalon and the nearby strongholds. He turned to Joppa and seized it before the enemy could,
for he had heard that its people were about to hand the stronghold over to the supporters of Demetrius. He stationed a garrison there to guard it.
When Jonathan returned, he called together the elders of the people and planned with them to build strongholds in Judea,
to build the walls of Jerusalem higher, and to raise a tall wall between citadel and city, cutting the citadel off so that it would stand alone and its garrison could neither buy nor sell.
So they gathered to build. Part of the wall along the ravine to the east had fallen, and he repaired the section called Chaphenatha.{g}
And Simon built Adida{h} in the Shephelah,{i} fortifying it and fitting it with gates and bars.
Then Trypho sought to become king of Asia, to put on the crown, and to lay hands on King Antiochus.
But he was afraid that Jonathan would not allow him and would make war on him. So he sought a way to seize and kill him, and he set out and came to Beth-shan.{j}
Jonathan went out to meet him with forty thousand picked men in battle array, and he too came to Beth-shan.
When Trypho saw that Jonathan had come with a large army, he was afraid to raise a hand against him.
Instead he welcomed him with honor, commended him to all his Friends, and gave him gifts. He ordered his Friends and his troops to obey Jonathan as they would himself.
Then he said to Jonathan, "Why have you put all these people to so much trouble, when there is no war between us?

Send them home now, and choose for yourself a few men to stay with you. Come with me to Ptolemais, and I will hand it over to you, along with the other strongholds, the rest of the troops, and all the officials. Then I will turn back and go home; that is why I have come."
Jonathan trusted him and did as he said. He dismissed his troops, and they went back to the land of Judah.
He kept with him three thousand men, of whom he left two thousand in Galilee, while a thousand went with him.
But as soon as Jonathan entered Ptolemais, the townspeople barred the gates and took him prisoner, and every man who had come in with him they put to the sword.
Trypho then sent troops and cavalry into Galilee and the Great Plain{k} to destroy all Jonathan's men.
These, believing that Jonathan had been seized and had perished along with his companions, encouraged one another and marched in close order, ready for battle.
Their pursuers, seeing that these men would sell their lives dearly, gave up the chase.
So all of them reached the land of Judah safely. They mourned for Jonathan and those with him, and they were in great fear; all Israel mourned deeply.
And all the nations around them sought to destroy them, for they said, "They have no leader or helper. Now let us make war on them and blot out their memory from among humankind."

notes.text: The Spartans, citizens of Sparta (Lacedaemon) in southern Greece.
Arius (Areus) I, king of Sparta 309–265 BC; Onias I was high priest about 320–290 BC.
The tradition of kinship between Spartans and Jews is also found in 2 Maccabees 5:9 and Josephus (Antiquities 12.226).
The region around Hamath on the Orontes, in Syria.
The fires were meant to make it look as if the camp was still occupied while the enemy withdrew (vv. 29–30); some ancient witnesses add "and withdrew."
An Arab tribe, perhaps near Zabdani northwest of Damascus.
The meaning of Chaphenatha is uncertain; perhaps Aramaic for "the double one."
Adida, Hebrew Hadid (Ezra 2:33), near Lydda.
The Shephelah, "lowland," the foothills between the Judean hills and the coastal plain.
Greek: Bethsan, Hebrew Beth-shan, "house of quiet" (Greek name Scythopolis).
The Great Plain, the plain of Jezreel (Esdraelon).

verses.text: Simon heard that Trypho had raised a large army to invade the land of Judah and lay it waste.
He saw that the people were trembling with fear, so he went up to Jerusalem and gathered them together.
He encouraged them, saying, "You yourselves know what great things I and my brothers and my father's house have done for the laws and the sanctuary, and what wars and hardships we have seen.
For this cause all my brothers have perished for Israel's sake, and I alone am left.
And now, far be it from me to spare my own life in any time of distress, for I am no better than my brothers.
Rather I will avenge my nation and the sanctuary and our wives and children, for all the nations have gathered out of hatred to crush us."
Hearing these words, the people took fresh heart,
and they answered with a loud shout, "You are our leader in place of Judas and Jonathan your brother.
Fight our battles, and whatever you tell us, we will do."
So he assembled all the fighting men and hurried to finish the walls of Jerusalem, and he fortified it on every side.
He sent Jonathan son of Absalom to Joppa with a sizable force; he drove out its inhabitants and remained there.
Then Trypho marched out of Ptolemais at the head of a great force to enter Judah's land, and Jonathan was with him as a prisoner.
Simon encamped at Adida, facing the plain.
When Trypho learned that Simon had risen up in place of his brother Jonathan and meant to join battle with him, he sent envoys to him with this message:
"We are holding your brother Jonathan because of silver he owed to the king's treasury for the posts he had.
Send now about four tons of silver{a} and two of his sons as hostages, so that when he is released he will not revolt against us, and we will release him."
Simon knew that they were speaking to him deceitfully, but he sent for the money and the boys, lest he bring great hostility on himself from the people,
lest they say, "Jonathan died because Simon would not send the silver and the boys."
So he sent the boys and the silver, but Trypho broke his word and did not release Jonathan.
After this Trypho came to invade the country and destroy it. He went around by the road to Adora,{b} but Simon and his army kept pace with him wherever he went.
The citadel garrison, for their part, sent messenger after messenger to Trypho, pressing him to reach them through the wilderness and get food to them.
So Trypho made ready all his cavalry to go, but that night there was a very heavy snowfall, and because of the snow he did not go. He set out and went into Gilead.
When he drew near Baskama,{c} he killed Jonathan, and he was buried there.
Then Trypho turned back and went to his own land.
Simon sent and recovered the bones of his brother Jonathan and buried him at Modein, the town of his ancestors.
All Israel lamented him with great lamentation and mourned for him many days.
Over the tomb of his father and his brothers Simon built a monument, high enough to be seen, with polished stone at back and front.
He erected seven pyramids, one opposite another, for his father and mother and four brothers.

For the pyramids he devised an elaborate setting: he set great columns around them, and on the columns he placed suits of armor as an everlasting memorial, and beside the armor carved ships, so that they could be seen by all who sail the sea.
This tomb that he built at Modein remains to this day.
Trypho dealt treacherously with the young King Antiochus; he killed him
and reigned in his place. He put on the crown of Asia and brought great disaster on the land.
But Simon built up the strongholds of Judea, girding them with high towers and great walls, with gates and bars, and he stored food in the strongholds.
Simon also chose men and sent them to King Demetrius, asking him to grant the land relief, for all that Trypho did was plunder.
King Demetrius answered him in line with this request, writing him the following letter:
"King Demetrius to Simon, high priest and Friend of kings, and to the elders and nation of the Jews, greetings.
The golden crown has reached us, and the palm branch{d} you sent, and we stand ready to make a lasting peace with you and to write to our officials to grant you exemptions.
All the agreements we have made with you stand, and the strongholds that you have built shall be yours.
We pardon any errors and offenses committed up to this day, and we cancel the crown tax that you owed; and whatever other tax was collected in Jerusalem shall be collected no longer.
If any of you are fit to be enrolled in our bodyguard, let them be enrolled, and let there be peace between us."
In the year 170 (142 BC){e} the yoke of the Gentiles was lifted from Israel,
and the people began to write in their documents and contracts, "In the first year of Simon, great high priest, commander and leader of the Jews."
In those days Simon{f} camped against Gaza{g} and surrounded it with troops. He built a siege tower, brought it up to the city, battered one of the towers, and captured it.
The men in the siege tower leaped out into the city, and a great uproar arose in the city.
The townspeople, wives and children with them, climbed onto the wall, rending their garments, and shouted aloud, begging Simon to make peace with them.
"Do not treat us as our wicked deeds deserve," they said, "but as your mercy allows."
So Simon came to terms with them and did not fight them. But he expelled them from the city and cleansed the houses in which there were idols, and then he entered it with hymns and praise.
He cast out all uncleanness from it and settled in it men who observe the law. He strengthened its fortifications and built a residence there for himself.
The garrison of the citadel in Jerusalem, cut off from going out to the countryside to buy and sell, suffered severe hunger, and many of them died of starvation.
They called out to Simon for terms of peace, and he granted them. He expelled them from there and cleansed the citadel from its pollutions.

On the twenty-third day of the second month (in April–May) in the year 171 (141 BC),{h} the Jews entered it with praise and palm branches, with lyres and cymbals and harps, with hymns and songs, because a great enemy had been crushed and removed from Israel.
He made it a law that this day be kept with gladness year by year. The temple mount beside the citadel he made still stronger, and there he made his home, he and his men.
Seeing that his son John{i} had reached manhood, Simon made him commander of all the forces, and he lived at Gazara.

notes.text: Greek: one hundred talents, about 7,500 lb (3,400 kg). Weight standards varied.
Adora (Adoraim, 2 Chronicles 11:9), southwest of Hebron.
Location unknown; probably northeast of the Sea of Galilee.
Greek baïn, a palm branch, perhaps of gold, given as a token of homage.
Greek: in the 170th year (Seleucid era; see note on 1:10).
Greek: he; Simon is meant.
So Swete's Greek text; many editors read Gazara (Gezer), following v. 53, 14:7, and Josephus, since Gaza lay outside Simon's territory.
Greek: the twenty-third of the second month of the 171st year (Seleucid era; see note on 1:10). The second month is Iyyar (April–May).
John Hyrcanus, ruler of Judea 134–104 BC.

verses.text: In the year 172 (140 BC){a} King Demetrius assembled his forces and marched into Media to gain reinforcements for his war against Trypho.
When Arsaces,{b} king of Persia and Media, heard that Demetrius had entered his territory, he sent one of his commanders to take him alive.
The commander went, defeated the army of Demetrius, seized him, and brought him to Arsaces, who put him under guard.

Crowning all his honors, he took Joppa for a harbor
and opened a way to the islands of the sea.

He enlarged the frontiers of his people
and held the land firmly in his grip.

He gathered in a host of captives;
he became master of Gazara, Beth-zur, and the citadel,
and removed its uncleanness from it,
and there was none to withstand him.

Old men sat in the streets,
all talking together of good things,
and the young men put on splendid garments and the dress of war.

He supplied the towns with food
and furnished them with means of defense,
until the fame of his glory was spoken of to the ends of the earth.

He established peace in the land,
and Israel rejoiced with great joy.

Each sat under his own vine and his own fig tree,{c}
and there was none to make them afraid.

None remained in the land to wage war on them;
in those days kings were broken.

He brought splendor to the holy place
and increased its sacred furnishings.
News of Jonathan's death reached Rome and even Sparta, and there was deep sorrow.
But once they learned that Simon his brother had taken his place as high priest and was ruling over the country and the towns in it,
they wrote to him on bronze tablets to renew with him the friendship and alliance they had established with his brothers Judas and Jonathan.
And these were read before the assembly in Jerusalem.

This is a copy of the letter that the Spartans sent:
"The rulers and the city of the Spartans to Simon the high priest, and to the elders, the priests, and the rest of the Jewish people, our brothers, greetings.
The envoys sent to our people have told us of your glory and honor, and we were glad at their coming.

Their report we have entered among the people's resolutions, in these words: 'Numenius son of Antiochus and Antipater son of Jason, Jewish envoys, have come before us to renew their friendship with us.

Our people resolved to welcome these men with honor and to lay up a copy of their words in the public records, as a memorial for the Spartan people.' And they have written a copy of this to Simon the high priest."
After this Simon sent Numenius to Rome with a great golden shield weighing about 1,250 pounds,{d} to confirm the alliance with the Romans.
Hearing of these events, the people asked, "What thanks can we give to Simon and his sons?

For he and his brothers and his father's house have stood firm; they have fought and driven off Israel's enemies and secured its freedom." So they inscribed this on bronze tablets and set them on a pillar on Mount Zion.

This is a copy of the inscription:
"On the eighteenth day of Elul (in August–September) in the year 172 (140 BC),{e} which is the third year of Simon the great high priest,
at Asaramel,{f} in the great assembly of the priests and the people, the nation's rulers, and the elders of the land, this was made known to us:

'Since wars have often arisen in the country, Simon son of Mattathias, a priest of the line of Joarib,{g} together with his brothers, put themselves in peril and stood against their nation's foes, to keep their sanctuary and the law standing; and they won high renown for their people.
Jonathan rallied the nation and became their high priest, and then he was gathered to his people.
When their enemies resolved to invade their country and lay it waste, and to lay hands on their sanctuary,
then Simon rose up and fought for his nation. He spent much of his own wealth; he armed the soldiers of his nation and paid their wages.
Judea's towns he fortified, and Beth-zur too, on Judea's frontier, which had once been the enemy's arsenal, and there he posted Jews as a garrison.

He fortified Joppa by the sea, and Gazara on the borders of Azotus, where the enemy had formerly lived. There he planted Jewish settlers and furnished the towns with all they required for their rebuilding.

The people saw how faithful Simon was and what glory he meant to bring his nation, and they chose him as their leader and high priest for all that he had done, and for the uprightness and good faith he had kept toward his people. He sought in every way to exalt his people.

In his days things prospered in his hands, so that the Gentiles were driven out of the country, and likewise the men in the City of David at Jerusalem, who had made a citadel for themselves and would go out from it to pollute the area around the sanctuary, doing great damage to its purity.
He settled Jews in it and fortified it for the safety of the country and of the city, and he raised the walls of Jerusalem higher.
For these reasons King Demetrius confirmed his high priesthood,
made him one of his Friends, and paid him high honors.
For he had heard that the Jews were addressed by the Romans as friends, allies, and brothers, and that the Romans had received Simon's envoys with honor.
The Jews and the priests have been pleased to have Simon as their leader and high priest for all time, till a prophet worthy of trust should appear,{h}
and that he should be commander over them and take charge of the sanctuary, appointing officials over its tasks and over the country, the weapons, and the strongholds;
that he should take charge of the sanctuary, and be obeyed by all; that all contracts in the country should be written in his name; and that he should be clothed in purple and wear gold.

None of the people or the priests shall be permitted to nullify any of these decisions, or to contradict what he says, or to convene an assembly in the country without him, or to be clothed in purple or wear a gold buckle.
Anyone who goes against these terms or sets any of them aside shall be held guilty.'
The whole people consented to let Simon act on these terms.
So Simon accepted, and agreed to serve as high priest and as general and ethnarch{i} of the Jews and the priests, and to stand at the head of all."
They gave orders that this inscription be placed on bronze tablets and set up in the precincts of the sanctuary in a prominent place,
and that copies of it be deposited in the treasury, so that Simon and his sons might have them.

notes.text: Greek: in the 172nd year (Seleucid era; see note on 1:10).
Arsaces, the royal title of the Parthian kings; here Mithradates I (about 171–138 BC).
Compare Micah 4:4 and 1 Kings 4:25.
Greek: a thousand minas, about 1,250 lb (570 kg); the mina was one sixtieth of a talent, and standards varied.
Greek: the eighteenth of Elul, of the 172nd year (Seleucid era; see note on 1:10). Elul is the sixth month (August–September).
So Swete's Greek text (Saramel in some ancient witnesses). The meaning is uncertain; perhaps Hebrew for "court of the people of God," or a title, "prince of the people of God."

verses.text: Antiochus son of King Demetrius{a} sent a letter from the islands of the sea to Simon, priest and ethnarch of the Jews, and to the whole nation.

Its contents were as follows:
"King Antiochus to Simon the great priest and ethnarch, and to the nation of the Jews, greetings.

Whereas certain pestilent men have made themselves masters of my fathers' kingdom, and it is my purpose to reclaim that kingdom and set it back as it once stood, I have recruited a host of troops and fitted out warships.
I mean to land in the country so that I may go after those who have ruined our country and laid waste many towns in my kingdom.
Now therefore I confirm to you all the tax remissions that the kings before me granted you, and whatever other exemptions they gave you.
You may strike coins of your own, to be the currency of your land.{b}
Jerusalem and the sanctuary shall be free. All the weapons you have made and the strongholds you have built and now hold shall remain yours.
Every debt you owe to the royal treasury, and any royal dues that may arise hereafter, are canceled for you from now on and for all time.
And when we have regained our kingdom, we will bestow great honor on you, your nation, and the temple, so that your glory will be made plain in all the earth."
In the year 174 (138 BC){c} Antiochus marched into the land of his ancestors. The troops came over to him in a body, until only a few remained on Trypho's side.
With King Antiochus in pursuit, Trypho fled and reached Dor{d} on the seacoast;
for he knew that troubles had piled up against him and that his troops had deserted him.
Antiochus pitched camp against Dor with a hundred twenty thousand fighting men and eight thousand horsemen.
He encircled the town, and the ships closed in from the sea. So he pressed the town hard by land and sea and let no one go out or come in.
Then Numenius and his companions arrived from Rome, bringing letters to the kings and countries, in which was written the following:
"Lucius,{e} consul of the Romans, to King Ptolemy,{f} greetings.
The envoys of the Jews have come to us as our friends and allies to renew the old friendship and alliance. They were sent by Simon the high priest and by the Jewish people,
and they have brought a gold shield weighing about 6,250 pounds.{g}

We have therefore resolved to write to the kings and countries that they should not seek to harm them, nor make war on them or their towns or their country, nor give help to any who fight against them.
It is our decision to receive the shield at their hands.
If, then, any pestilent men have escaped from their land and taken refuge with you, deliver them up to Simon the high priest, so that he may punish them according to their law."
Letters to the same effect went to King Demetrius,{h} to Attalus,{i} Ariarathes,{j} and Arsaces,

and to all the countries: to Sampsames,{k} to the Spartans, and to Delos, Myndos, Sicyon, Caria, Samos, Pamphylia, Lycia, Halicarnassus, Cos, Side, Arados, Rhodes, Phaselis, Gortyn, Cnidus, Cyprus, and Cyrene.{l}
And a copy of the whole was written out for Simon the high priest.
King Antiochus besieged Dor in its outskirts,{m} continually throwing his forces against it and building siege engines; and he shut Trypho in, so that no one could go out or in.
Simon sent him two thousand picked men to fight on his side, along with silver and gold and a good deal of equipment.
But Antiochus would not accept them. He broke every agreement he had made with Simon before and turned against him.
He sent Athenobius, one of his Friends, to confer with him, saying, "You hold Joppa and Gazara and the citadel in Jerusalem, which are towns of my kingdom.
You have laid waste their territory, done great harm to the land, and made yourselves masters of many places in my kingdom.
Now then, hand over the towns you have seized, and the tribute of the places you have taken outside the borders of Judea;

or else give me in their place about nineteen tons of silver,{n} and for the destruction you have caused and for the tribute of the towns, another nineteen tons. Otherwise we will come and make war on you."

So Athenobius, the king's Friend, came to Jerusalem. When he saw the splendor of Simon, his sideboard laden with gold and silver vessels, and his great retinue, he was astounded. He gave him the king's message.
Simon answered him, "We have neither taken foreign land nor seized anything that belongs to others, but only the inheritance of our ancestors, which our enemies at one time unjustly took.
Now that we have the opportunity, we are holding firmly to the inheritance of our ancestors.

As for Joppa and Gazara, which you demand, those towns were doing great harm among our people and in our land; for them we will give about four tons of silver."{o} Athenobius did not answer him a word,
but returned in a rage to the king and reported to him these words, the splendor of Simon, and all he had seen. And the king was furious.
Meanwhile Trypho boarded a ship and fled to Orthosia.{p}
Then the king made Cendebeus commander-in-chief of the coastal region and gave him troops of infantry and cavalry.
He ordered him to encamp facing Judea, to rebuild Kedron{q} and strengthen the towns,{r} and to wage war on the people, while the king pursued Trypho.
So Cendebeus came to Jamnia and began to provoke the people, invading Judea, taking the people captive, and killing them.
At Kedron, which he rebuilt, he posted cavalry and troops to sally out and patrol the roads of Judea, as the king had ordered him.

verses.text: Coming up from Gazara, John reported to Simon his father all that Cendebeus was about.

Simon summoned his two eldest sons, Judas and John, and said to them, "From our youth until this day, I and my brothers and my father's house have fought Israel's wars, and time and again we have succeeded in rescuing Israel.
But now I have grown old, while you, by Heaven's mercy, are of full age. Stand in my place and my brother's; march out and do battle on behalf of our people, and may aid from heaven go with you."
So John chose from the country twenty thousand fighting men and horsemen, and they marched against Cendebeus and spent the night at Modein.
Rising early, they advanced into the plain, where a great host of foot and horse came marching against them, with a stream between the two armies.
John and his men took up position facing the enemy. Seeing that his men were afraid to cross the stream, he crossed over first; and when the men saw him, they crossed after him.
He divided his army, placing the horsemen in the midst of the foot soldiers, for the enemy's cavalry was very numerous.
They sounded the trumpets, and Cendebeus and his army were put to flight. Many of them fell wounded, and the rest fled to the stronghold.
It was then that John's brother Judas was wounded; but John pursued the enemy until he came to Kedron, which Cendebeus had built.
They fled to the towers in the fields of Azotus, and John burned it{a} with fire. About a thousand of them fell, and he returned to Judea in safety.
Now Ptolemy son of Abubus had been appointed governor over the plain of Jericho, and he had a great deal of silver and gold,
for he was the high priest's son-in-law.
His heart grew proud, and he resolved to make himself master of the country; so he plotted treachery against Simon and his sons, to do away with them.

Simon was making a tour of the towns of the country, attending to their needs. He went down to Jericho with his sons Mattathias and Judas in the year 177 (134 BC), in the eleventh month (in January–February), which is the month of Shebat.{b}
The son of Abubus received them with guile in the small fort he had built, named Dok.{c} There he held a great drinking feast for them, having hidden men in the place.
When Simon and his sons were drunk, Ptolemy and his men rose up, took their weapons, rushed in upon Simon in the banquet hall, and killed him, his two sons, and some of his servants.
So he committed a great act of treachery and repaid good with evil.
Then Ptolemy put these things in writing and dispatched it to the king, urging him to send forces to his support and to hand over to him their country and towns.
He sent other men to Gazara to do away with John, and he sent letters to the officers of the thousands, inviting them to come to him so that he might give them silver, gold, and gifts.
Still others he sent to take possession of Jerusalem and the temple hill.
But a messenger outran them and told John at Gazara that his father and brothers were dead, and said, "He has sent men to kill you too."
At this news John was greatly shaken. He seized the men who came to destroy him and killed them, for he had learned that they were seeking to destroy him.
The rest of the acts of John, his wars and the brave deeds he did, the building of the walls that he built, and his other achievements,
are written in the annals of his high priesthood, from the time he became high priest after his father.{d}
